facts.name: 90 Mile Beach
facts.windOffshore: ENE (surfnerd wind exposure NNE - ESE, "Offshore from ENE"); NE (surfnerd guide text: "northeast (NE) offshore wind")
facts.notes: Surfnerd overview: 90 Mile Beach is one of the longest virgin beaches on earth, a vast stretch of sand that doubles as a marked National Highway at low tide. It's a beach break that peels both left and right over sand, and The Bluff, the only headland about two-thirds of the way up, is the standout bank. Skill (surfnerd): Beginner. Access (surfnerd): Getting here means driving the beach at low tide, and a 4WD is crucial. Soft sand and incoming tides catch plenty of people out, and many get stuck. There's road access from Te Kao, free parking, and a rudimentary campsite if you want to stay.

facts.notes: Surfnerd overview: Airport Reef sits off the end of the Wellington Airport runway and breakwater, out from Lyall Bay. A big peak throws up both rights and lefts, dredging into a gnarly drop before opening onto a fat wall. It breaks over boulders and rock, part reef and part beach, and heavy close-outs come with the territory. This is a serious wave best left to experienced surfers. Surf-forecast Airport-Rights_1: "Airport Rights in Wellington is an exposed reef break that has inconsistent surf. Summer in particular tends to be flat. Offshore winds are from the north and there is no shelter here from cross shore breezes. Most of the surf here comes from groundswells and the best swell direction is from the south. There is no reef break. Unlikely to be too crowded, even when the surf is up. Watch out for rocks and obstacles." Other guide pins from this position: surf-forecast Airport-Rights_1 1.0 km.

facts.name: Albatross Point
facts.windOffshore: SSW (surfnerd wind exposure SSE - WSW, "Offshore from SSW"); S (surfnerd guide text: "south (S) offshore wind")
facts.notes: Surfnerd overview: Albatross Point is a remote left-hand point that breaks over uneven reef. It needs a huge swell to refract around into Arohaki Bay, where it fans out into multiple left points, and it rewards the effort with a genuinely good wave when it all comes together. Check: surfnerd states facing NNE but best swell SW (157.5 degrees apart); both are as published. Skill (surfnerd): Intermediate. Access (surfnerd): Getting here is the hard part. The overland route runs southwest from Hamilton toward Taharoa, and from there you need to see the farmer about crossing his land, so knowing someone who can negotiate that permission is essential. The alternative is a boat from Kawhia Harbour, which again relies on local knowledge. Parking is restricted.

facts.notes: Surfnerd overview: Amberley Beach is a punchy, fun beach break spread along a shingle and stone shoreline on the coast out from Amberley township, north of Christchurch. Several peaks line the beach with both rights and lefts, so there's room to pick a section that suits you. It's a modest spot rather than a standout, but the waves carry real bite when they're on. Surf-forecast Amberley-Beach: "Amberley Beach in Canterbury is an exposed beach break that has fairly consistent surf and can work at any time of the year. Works best in offshore winds from the west northwest and there is no shelter here from cross shore breezes. Easily blown out by onshore winds Most of the surf here comes from groundswells and the best swell direction is from the east southeast. The beach break offers both left and right hand waves. The location means that it never gets crowded. Watch out for dangerous rips." Access (surfnerd): At the north end of the beach sits Fossils, a left-hand point break and beach break. Reaching it takes a 4WD or a very long walk, so plan for the effort if you want to surf there. Other guide pins from this position: surf-forecast Amberley-Beach 2.2 km.

facts.notes: Surfnerd overview: Back Beach is a powerful, peaky beachbreak just outside New Plymouth, and it's where local surfers head to make the most of the swell. The waves break both left and right over sand, and on the push you can find long, tapered walls to work down. The banks at the north end are good enough to host regular contests. Check: surfnerd states facing WNW but best swell SW (67.5 degrees apart); both are as published. Skill (surfnerd): Beginner. Surf-forecast Back-Beach_1: "Back Beach in Taranaki is a fairly exposed beach break that has reasonably consistent surf. Autumn and winter are the optimum times of year for waves. Offshore winds are from the east. Windswells and groundswells in equal measure and the ideal swell direction is from the west southwest. Both left and right reef breaks. Best around high tide when the tide is rising. It very rarely gets crowded here. Take care of the strong rips here." Access (surfnerd): From New Plymouth city centre, head southwest on Devon Street West (the Surf Highway, State Highway 45), then turn right onto Lawry Street and left onto Breakwater Road. Near the port, turn left onto Ngamotu Road and take the first right onto Centennial Drive. Follow it down and, just past Rangitake Drive, turn right into the Back Beach car park. There's free parking in the car park plus roadside parking, and restrooms on hand. Other guide pins from this position: surf-forecast Back-Beach_1 0.2 km.

facts.notes: Surfnerd overview: Beatons is a grinding left pointbreak that peels over rocky reef down in New Zealand's deep south. When it lines up, it serves a mix of barrels and walls, making it one of the more rewarding lefts in the area for those equipped to surf it. Check: surfnerd states facing WNW but best swell S (112.5 degrees apart); both are as published. Skill (surfnerd): Expert. Surf-forecast Beatons: "Beatons in Invercargill is an exposed point break that has fairly consistent surf and can work at any time of the year. Offshore winds blow from the northeast. Waves just as likely from local windswells as from distant groundswells and the ideal swell angle is from the south.The waves is a point break that peels left. Best around low tide when the tide is rising. Unlikely to be too crowded, even when the surf is up. Beware of sharks/rips." Access (surfnerd): Getting to Beatons takes some effort and a bit of courtesy. From Invercargill, head north out of town on North Road (State Highway 6), then turn left onto Wallacetown Lorneville Highway (State Highway 99). Continue through Wallacetown and Riverton, turn left onto Pahia-Wakapatu Road, then right onto Garden Road, and follow it to the end to park. From there it is a walk across the paddock out to the point. The beach is only reachable across farmland, so you must ask the farmer for permission to cross the land before heading out. There is free parking at the road, though roadside parking is restricted, so leave your car considerately. Other guide pins from this position: surf-forecast Beatons 0.6 km.

facts.notes: Surfnerd overview: Bell Block is a powerful left-hand reef near New Plymouth on New Zealand's North Island, breaking over an uneven reef. The outside left runs hollow and carries serious power, but it takes a big swell and a long paddle to reach, so it's firmly a wave for experienced surfers. Closer to shore, an inside beachbreak gives beginners a more forgiving option and works nicely at mid tide until the beach disappears at high. Check: surfnerd states facing N but best swell SW (135 degrees apart); both are as published. Skill (surfnerd): Expert. Surf-forecast Bell-Block-Reef: "Bell Block Reef in Taranaki is a fairly exposed reef break that only works once in a while. Autumn and winter are the best times of year for waves. Offshore winds blow from the southeast. Windswells and groundswells in equal measure and the optimum swell angle is from the west southwest. A left hand reef break. Best around low tide. Unlikely to be too crowded, even when the surf is up. Hazards include urchins and rocks." Access (surfnerd): From New Plymouth city centre, head east on Devon Street East and continue onto State Highway 3 out of town. At Bell Block, turn left onto Mangati Road and follow it down to the beach, where you'll find a car park and restrooms. Other guide pins from this position: surf-forecast Bell-Block-Reef 0.9 km.

facts.name: Big Ning Nong
facts.windOffshore: NE (surfnerd wind exposure N - E, "Offshore from NE"); NE (surfnerd guide text: "northeast (NE) offshore wind")
facts.notes: Surfnerd overview: Big Ning Nong is a big left-hand point break out near the end of Cape Palliser, before you reach Black Rocks. It's the outermost of several waves strung along the same point: Raspberries sits furthest inside, Little Ning Nong is the left closer to shore, and Craps is the A-frame out on the point. Big Ning Nong itself is the outer reef beyond them all, so it's worth being clear that the name means the big left out the back, past Craps. It breaks over rock, and when it's on, it's one of the standout waves here.

Don't be surprised by the piles of large driftwood logs scattered along the beach.

It very rarely gets crowded here. Surfing here means negotiating dangerous rips." Access (surfnerd): Getting out takes a bit of effort. facts.notes: Surfnerd overview: Colac Bay is a beginner-friendly beachbreak on New Zealand's south coast, offering both lefts and rights over a mix of uneven reef and sand. It is a forgiving spot to learn on, and while it rates below average overall, it has its worthwhile windows. At the south end sits Nicks Point, a righthand walling wave that needs at least 3 ft of swell to clear the rocky coastline. Skill (surfnerd): Beginner. Surf-forecast Colac-Bay: "Colac Bay in Invercargill is an exposed beach break that has quite reliable surf and can work at any time of the year. The best wind direction is from the northwest. Tends to receive a mix of groundswells and windswells and the best swell direction is from the south. The beach break offers both left and right hand waves. Surfable at all stages of the tide. It very rarely gets crowded here. Take care of rips, rocks and sharks." Access (surfnerd): There is a car park with free parking near the beach, and camping is available if you want to stay close to the water. From Invercargill, head north on North Road (State Highway 6), then turn left onto the Wallacetown Lorneville Highway (State Highway 99). Continue through Wallacetown and Riverton, and at Colac turn left on either Colac Bay Road or Colac Foreshore Road. Follow Colac Foreshore Road southwest to the end of the bay and park near the beach. Other guide pins from this position: surf-forecast Colac-Bay 0.8 km.

facts.name: Craps
facts.windOffshore: NE (surfnerd wind exposure N - E, "Offshore from NE"); NE (surfnerd guide text: "northeast (NE) offshore wind")
facts.notes: Surfnerd overview: Craps is an A-frame reef peak sitting off the very end of the point at Cape Palliser, just before you reach Black Rocks. It's one of a cluster of breaks strung along the same point, each with its own name: Raspberries and Little Ning Nong peel as left-handers on the inside, while Big Ning Nong is the outer reef that only comes to life on big swells. Craps holds down the tip of the point and serves up both rights and lefts. The left is the standout, a powerful, good-quality wave with a steep drop-in and several distinct sections. The right is a different animal: fast, short, and a hollow barrel. It's a break for intermediate to expert surfers, and when it's on it ranks among the best waves around.

Access (surfnerd): Getting here takes some effort. From Whangarei, head north on Western Hills Drive (State Highway 1), turn right onto Russell Road, then left to stay on Russell Road, and right onto Rawhiti Road, following it round to Elliot Bay and down to the beach. The final stretch crosses private farmland, where an honesty box on the fence lets you pay your way in. Parking is restricted, and you'll find more pristine, isolated breaks scattered to the north. Access (surfnerd): From Wanganui, head north on London Street, Great North Road and State Highway 3. At Waitotara, turn left onto Trent Street, continue onto Ihupuku Street and Waiinu Beach Road, and drop down to Waiinu Beach. From there, either take the track east about 1 km along the beach or walk in. If you drive down the track, shut the farm gates behind you; otherwise walk from Waiinu Beach. Parking is free, with roadside spots available.

facts.notes: Surfnerd overview: Gizzy Pipe is a sand-bottomed beach break at Midway Beach in Gisborne. Closer to the river, Waikanae and Midway offer easy, beginner-friendly waves, but the real draw is out where the town's sewer pipe runs 3 km offshore. The outfall has shaped top-quality sandbars that throw fast, thumping tubes, which is what puts this peak on the map. Skill (surfnerd): Expert. Surf-forecast Midway-Beach: "Midway Beach in Gisborne is a fairly exposed beach break that usually has waves and can work at any time of the year. Offshore winds are from the north. Clean groundswells prevail and the best swell direction is from the south southeast. The beach breaks offer lefts and rights. Best around mid tide when the tide is rising. When the surf is up, it can get quite busy in the water. Beware of ." Surf-forecast Gizzy-Pipe: "Midway Beach - Gizzy Pipe in Gisborne and Mahia is an exposed beach break that has dependable surf and can work at any time of the year. The best wind direction is from the north northwest and there is no shelter here from cross shore breezes. Groundswells more frequent than windswells and the best swell direction is from the south southeast. The beach break provides left and right handers. Best around low tide. When the surf is up, it can get quite busy in the water. Take care of rips and pollution." Access (surfnerd): From Gisborne city centre, near the clock tower on Gladstone Road, head west, turn south onto Stanley Road, and follow it to the end at the Midway Surf Life Saving Club beside Watson Park. Turn right onto Centennial Marine Drive and find a park a little further along. The main peak sits a few hundred metres west down the beach from the surf club. There is a car park with free parking plus roadside parking, and the spot is well set up with restrooms, showers, camping, a lifeguard, a surf school, and a surf shop. Other guide pins from this position: surf-forecast Midway-Beach 1.2 km, surf-forecast Gizzy-Pipe 2.7 km.

At Domett, turn right onto Hururnui Mouth Road, then left onto Cathedral Road and over to Gore Bay. Alternatively, carry on into Cheviot and turn right onto Gore Bay Road, which also leads in. There's a car park with free parking plus roadside parking, and beach facilities include restrooms, showers, and a lifeguard. A couple of campgrounds make it easy to stay longer if you want to. Follow the gravel road across the railway line toward the cemetery, where the right-handers break in front of the graveyard. There's free roadside parking.

facts.windOffshore: NW (surfnerd wind exposure W - N, "Offshore from NW"); NW (surfnerd guide text: "northwest (NW) offshore wind"); North (surf-forecast)
facts.notes: Surfnerd overview: Hickory Bay is the most consistent beachbreak on this stretch of the peninsula, breaking over sand and earning a solid reputation among the local waves. Good lefts wedge up in the north corner near the cliffs, throwing heavy, hollow walls. Those inside sections come with punishing paddle-outs once it gets overhead, a common theme along this coast. Skill (surfnerd): Intermediate. Surf-forecast Hickory-Bay: "Hickory Bay in Banks Peninsular is an exposed beach break that has quite reliable surf and can work at any time of the year. Offshore winds blow from the north. Windswells and groundswells in equal measure and the best swell direction is from the southeast. Waves at the beach break both left and right. It's sometimes crowded here. Take care of rips and rocks." Access (surfnerd): Getting in takes some effort. From Christchurch, head toward Akaroa on State Highway 75, turn left at the Takamatua Road hill and climb Long Bay Road to the Summit Road, then take the second left onto the gravel Hickory Bay Road. It's shingle, narrow, winding and bumpy, so take it easy on the way down. At the bottom there's a car park with free parking, plus roadside parking, and from there it's a 10-15 minute walk through a farm track and gates to the beach. Follow the signs and steer clear of the farmer's driveway. There are no facilities, no toilets, and no camping or fires, so come prepared and pack out everything you bring in. If you want smaller, empty conditions, nearby Goughs Bay is worth a look. Other guide pins from this position: surf-forecast Hickory-Bay 0.7 km.

The north end sometimes offers a left-hand point break, while the south end has a right-hand break off an outer reef. In the middle, natural hot springs bubble up in front of the rocks, and at low tide you will see people digging their own hot pools in the sand. Despite the name, the water itself can be quite cool, since there are cold springs under the surface too. Surf-forecast Hotwater-Beach: "Hot water Beach in Coromandel is a reasonably exposed beach and point break that has quite reliable surf. Spring and Summer provide the best conditions. Best around mid tide when the tide is rising. Unlikely to be too crowded, even when the surf is up. Beware of rocks and sharks." facts.name: Indicators (Raglan)
facts.windOffshore: SSE (surfnerd wind exposure ESE - SSW, "Offshore from SSE"); SE (surfnerd guide text: "southeast (SE) offshore wind"); Southeast (surf-forecast)
facts.notes: Surfnerd overview: Indicators is the longest, fastest and most critical of Raglan's three points, a left-hander that peels over boulders. On smaller days it splits into two or three separate sections. The Outside Indicators peak throws a heavy take-off into a throaty barrel and picks up the most size of the three points, though it also catches the most wind. Down the line, hollow sections trade off with open performance and cutback walls, before a final Valley section speeds up and hollows out again. On the biggest days the wave can occasionally break far enough out to link with Whale Bay, and sometimes Manu, though it rarely joins the dots for the full two kilometres. Check: surfnerd states facing NNW but best swell SW (112.5 degrees apart); both are as published. Skill (surfnerd): Expert. Surf-forecast Raglan-Indicators: "Raglan-Indicators in West Coast Auckland is an exposed point break that has reasonably consistent surf and can work at any time of the year. Offshore winds are from the southeast. Waves can be ok even in light onshore winds Waves just as likely from local windswells as from distant groundswells and the ideal swell direction is from the southwest.There is a left breaking point here. It's sometimes crowded here. Watch out for rocks and locals." Access (surfnerd): Getting out is a mission. Park near the end of Tohora Close, where the free roadside parking is limited and fills fast in summer, then take the walkway down to Whale Bay and follow the shoreline west to the next bay. From there you either paddle across from the lagoon or pick your way over the rocks. Restrooms are available. Other guide pins from this position: surf-forecast Raglan-Indicators 0.5 km.

facts.windOffshore: ENE (surfnerd wind exposure NNE - ESE, "Offshore from ENE"); NE (surfnerd guide text: "northeast (NE) offshore wind")
facts.notes: Surfnerd overview: Little Ning Nong is a left-hand point break out near the end of Cape Palliser, just before you reach Black Rocks. It's one of several waves sharing the same point, so it helps to know which is which: Little Ning Nong is the left closer to shore, Raspberries sits even further inside, Craps is the A-frame out on the point, and Big Ning Nong is the outer reef that only breaks on bigger swells. The wave itself peels over rock and is a good-quality, long left with several sections to work through.

Peaks are scattered all the way down the beach, giving you plenty of room to spread out and pick your spot, with both lefts and rights on offer. The waves come with a punchy drop and good wally walls, and the inside often throws a hollow shorey. Surf-forecast Little-Wanganui: "Little Wanganui in North West Coast is an exposed beach/river bar break that does not work very often with no particular seasonal pattern. Works best in offshore winds from the east. Most of the surf here comes from groundswells and the ideal swell angle is from the west northwest. The beach break offers both left and right hand waves. The quality of the surf isn't affected by the tide. Even when there are waves, it's not likley to be crowded. Be wary of rips - they make surfing here dangerous." facts.name: Loisells Beach
facts.windOffshore: WNW (surfnerd wind exposure WSW - NNW, "Offshore from WNW"); NW (surfnerd guide text: "northwest (NW) offshore wind"); Northwest (surf-forecast)
facts.tide: Low, Mid (surfnerd); Best around mid tide when the tide is falling. (surf-forecast)
facts.notes: Surfnerd overview: Loisells Beach, also known as Waihau Bay, is a set of exposed beachbreaks anchored by the odd rocky patch, with waves peeling over a mix of uneven reef and sand. It sits on a good stretch of coast and pulls in plenty of swell. A rock and sand point sits within walking distance to the north if you want to scout another option. Skill (surfnerd): Beginner. Surf-forecast Loisells: "Loisells in East Cape is a fairly exposed beach break that has quite consistent surf and can work at any time of the year. Offshore winds are from the north northwest. Groundswells more frequent than windswells and the best swell direction is from the northeast. Waves at the beach are both lefts and rights. Best around mid tide when the tide is falling. Relatively few surfers here, even on good days. Watch out for rips and rocks." Access (surfnerd): From Gisborne town centre, head east on Gladstone Road onto Wainui Road and State Highway 35 towards Wainui. Carry on past Wainui along Moana Road and onto Whangara Road, then at Waihau Bay turn right onto Waihau Road. The road turns to gravel and runs down to the beach. There's camping nearby, plus a car park with free parking and roadside parking. Other guide pins from this position: surf-forecast Loisells 0.9 km.

facts.name: Long Bay
facts.windOffshore: SW (surfnerd wind exposure S - W, "Offshore from SW"); SW (surfnerd guide text: "southwest (SW) offshore wind"); West-southwest (surf-forecast)
facts.notes: Surfnerd overview: Long Bay is a cluster of beaches in the suburb of Torbay, on Auckland's north shore on the east coast. The beaches themselves are mostly low-quality straighthanders, so the pick is the reef at the southern end below Cliff Road, which breaks over a mix of rock ledge and sand. It's a below-average spot overall, but the reef is worth knowing about for the right day. Skill (surfnerd): Beginner. Surf-forecast Long-Bay-Reef: "Long Bay Reef in Auckland is a sheltered reef break Offshore winds blow from the west southwest with some shelter here from southwest winds. Windswells and groundswells in equal measure and the ideal swell direction is from the east northeast. It's sometimes crowded here. Beware of - Urchins - Rocks." Access (surfnerd): Park on Cliff Road and the reef is right out in front, with restrooms on hand. Getting there from Auckland, head north on the Auckland Northern Motorway (State Highway 1) over the Auckland Harbour Bridge, take exit 410, then turn right onto Oteha Valley Road. Continue onto Carlisle Road, turn left onto Beach Road, then right onto Rewi Street to reach Cliff Road. Other guide pins from this position: surf-forecast Long-Bay-Reef 1.2 km.

facts.windOffshore: E (surfnerd wind exposure NE - SE, "Offshore from E"); N (surfnerd guide text: "north (N) offshore wind")
facts.notes: Surfnerd overview: Magnet Bay is a small, scenic cove that breaks left over boulders, surfed since the early 1960s by the Midshore Boardriders club. The lefts don't really wrap, but the walls can get pretty juicy and the rides can run a good length. It's a solid setup. Check: surfnerd states facing W but best swell S (90 degrees apart); both are as published. Skill (surfnerd): Intermediate. Access (surfnerd): From Christchurch, drive out through Halswell on Christchurch Akaroa Road (Highway 75), through Tai Tapu and past Birdlings Flat to Little River. As you enter Little River, turn right onto Wairewa Pa Road signposted to the southern bays, then take the first right onto Kinloch Road, which winds up the hill. At the summit the road turns to gravel; turn right onto Bossu Road, then first left onto Te Oka Bay Road. At the first farmer's house, turn right onto the signposted Magnet Bay Road. Park on the grass opposite the farmer's, with free roadside parking, then it's a short two-minute walk across the paddock to the beach.

facts.notes: Surfnerd overview: Mahia Spit is a long, skinny finger of rock that turns into something powerful and hollow down its eastern side. The outside section breaks square, super-shallow, and fast over uneven reef, so only experienced barrel-riders tend to make it out the other end. The right off the tip and the inside section are far more forgiving. Just north of Mahia town you'll also find Old Mans, a set of scattered, cliff-lined sand and reef peaks. Skill (surfnerd): Expert. Surf-forecast Mahia-Spit: "Mahia Spit in Mahia is an exposed reef break that does not work very often. Summer offers the best conditions for surfing. Offshore winds are from the southwest. Groundswells more frequent than windswells and the best swell direction is from the northeast. There is a left hand reef break. Rarely crowded here. Hazards include rocks and locals." Access (surfnerd): From Napier, follow State Highway 2 north through Wairoa to Nuhaka, then take Nuhaka Opoutama Road and Ormond Drive toward Mahia Beach. At Mahia Beach, continue onto Mahia East Coast Road, which cuts across to the peninsula's east coast; the rocky spit sits just south of Mahia and is hard to miss. There's a car park with free parking plus roadside parking, along with restrooms and camping. Other guide pins from this position: surf-forecast Mahia-Spit 1.1 km.

facts.name: Milford Reef
facts.windOffshore: WSW (surfnerd wind exposure SSW - WNW, "Offshore from WSW"); W (surfnerd guide text: "west (W) offshore wind"); West (surf-forecast)

facts.notes: Surfnerd overview: Milford Reef breaks at the southern end of Milford beach, in the suburb of Milford on Auckland's east coast, north of Devonport. Tufts of reef here hold the sand in place, so lefts and rights can form and peel instead of closing out like the rest of the beach. It's a modest setup that rates below average overall, but the reef gives it shape the open beach lacks. Skill (surfnerd): Beginner. Surf-forecast Milford-Beach: "Milford Beach in Auckland East Coast is a sheltered beach and reef break that only works once in a while. Spring and Summer provide the best conditions. The best wind direction is from the west. Tends to receive distant groundswells and the ideal swell angle is from the northeast. The beach break provides left and right handers and there are also left and right hand reef breaks on offer.. Best around high tide. When the surf is up, it can get quite busy in the water. Beware of rocks, locals and pollution." Access (surfnerd): From Auckland, head north on the Northern Motorway (State Highway 1) over the Harbour Bridge, take exit 419 and turn right onto Northcote Road. Turn left onto Taharoto Road, right onto Shakespeare Road, continue onto Omana Road, then straight onto Ihumata Road. Turn left onto Milford Road and follow it down to the beach; the reef sits right out front. All the facilities, including restrooms, are at the northern end. For parking, there's a car park with free parking, plus paid and roadside options. Other guide pins from this position: surf-forecast Milford-Beach 2.5 km.

facts.notes: Surfnerd overview: Motiti Island is a rocky island roughly 10 km off the Tauranga coastline, sitting out beyond Papamoa Beach. It holds several breaks around its tips. The southern tip serves up a right-hander alongside a beachbreak, while the north-eastern corner throws a left. That north-east break, known as Swannies, is a hollow, powerful left-hander. On the eastern side of the southern tip you'll find a punchy beachbreak with both lefts and rights, and the western side of the same tip offers a long, powerful right. This is expert-only surf. Surf-forecast Sannis: "Motiti Island - Kaiwakawaka ree in Bay of Plenty is an exposed beach break that has fairly consistent surf and can work at any time of the year. Offshore winds are from the south southwest and there is no shelter here from cross shore breezes. Easily blown out by onshore winds Groundswells more frequent than windswells and the ideal swell angle is from the east northeast. There is no beach break and there is a left hand reef break as well. Best around high tide. Even when there are waves, it's not likley to be crowded. Watch out for sharks." Surf-forecast Motiti-Island-Right: "Motiti Island Right in Bay of Plenty is a reasonably exposed beach break that has fairly consistent surf and can work at any time of the year. Offshore winds are from the south with some shelter here from east winds. Windswells and groundswells in equal measure and the best swell direction is from the northeast. There is no beach break and there is a right hand reef break as well. Best around high tide. It very rarely gets crowded here. Be warned that sharks have been sighted." Surf-forecast Ernies: "Motiti Island - Ernies in Bay of Plenty is an exposed beach break that has reasonably consistent surf and can work at any time of the year. Offshore winds blow from the west with some shelter here from northwest winds. Easily blown out by onshore winds Most of the surf here comes from groundswells and the ideal swell direction is from the east southeast. There is no beach break and there are also left and right hand reef breaks on offer. Best around high tide. Even when there are waves, it's not likley to be crowded. Be warned that sharks have been sighted." Other guide pins from this position: surf-forecast Sannis 1.6 km, surf-forecast Motiti-Island-Right 1.6 km, surf-forecast Ernies 2.3 km.

facts.notes: Surfnerd overview: Mount Maunganui Main Beach is a sandy, summer-popular stretch that offers two very different rides: beach-break peaks scattered along the sand, and a right-hand point that peels off Moturiki Island, the blowhole, at the south end. The shore break can turn sucky and hollow, so there is real punch close to the sand. Surf-forecast Mount-Maunguni: "Mount Maunguni in Bay of Plenty is a reasonably exposed beach break that has fairly consistent surf and can work at any time of the year. Offshore winds blow from the south southwest. Tends to receive distant groundswells and the best swell direction is from the north northeast. The beach break provides left and right handers. The quality of the surf isn't affected by the tide. When it's working here, it can get crowded. Take care of ." Other guide pins from this position: surf-forecast Mount-Maunguni 0.2 km.

facts.notes: Surfnerd overview: Mukies 1 is a left-hand point that peels over a mix of uneven reef and sand. It breaks consistently and holds up as a genuinely good wave, with a short, sucky barrel section as the standout when everything lines up. Check: surfnerd states facing NNE but best swell SW (157.5 degrees apart); both are as published. Skill (surfnerd): Intermediate. Access (surfnerd): Getting out means a long paddle from the beach, or you can find a gap in the rocks further up the point and let the constant drift carry you down. There's a car park with free parking.

It only shows a few times a year, but when it does the rights are epic: a mellow longboard wave when small, turning into a hollow racetrack at head-high with plenty of tube time once the sand lines up. Skill (surfnerd): Intermediate. Access (surfnerd): Parking is free, both off the road and roadside. Take care on the steep, slippery access road, and watch for rocks and sharks in the water.

facts.name: Muriwai Beach
facts.windOffshore: E (surfnerd wind exposure NE - SE, "Offshore from E"); E (surfnerd guide text: "east (E) offshore wind"); East (surf-forecast)
facts.tide: Low, Mid, High (surfnerd); Best around high tide when the tide is rising. (surf-forecast)
hazards: Overview Muriwai Beach is a shifty beach break where the peaks rely on constantly moving sandbars and strong rips for their shape. (surfnerd)
facts.notes: Surfnerd overview: Muriwai Beach is a shifty beach break where the peaks rely on constantly moving sandbars and strong rips for their shape. The left point to the south is prone to backwash in front of the rocks, so many surfers head round the corner to Maori Bay for better-defined peaks along the cliffy bay. Skill (surfnerd): Beginner. Surf-forecast Muriwai-Beach: "Muriwai Beach in West Coast Auckland is an exposed beach break that has very consistent surf and works all around the year. Offshore winds are from the east. Windswells and groundswells in equal measure and the ideal swell direction is from the southwest. Waves at the beach break both left and right. Best around high tide when the tide is rising. When the surf is up, it can get quite busy in the water. Take care of rips and sharks." Access (surfnerd): There's a car park with free parking, plus restrooms, showers, camping and lifeguard cover, and a big motor park behind the dunes. Gannet and seal colonies nearby attract other predators. Other guide pins from this position: surf-forecast Muriwai-Beach 2.2 km.

facts.name: Mussel Rock
facts.windOffshore: NE (surfnerd wind exposure N - E, "Offshore from NE"); NE (surfnerd guide text: "northeast (NE) offshore wind")
hazards: Keep an eye on the tide movement, though, because it drives the current and the speed of the paddle, which can turn genuinely terrifying when it's running hard. (surfnerd)
You either make the long, hard paddle across the current-swept harbour entrance from Raglan, or take a boat. (surfnerd)
facts.notes: Surfnerd overview: Mussel Rock is a sand-bottom beach break sitting across the harbour entrance from Raglan, and the banks that shift around the rocks give it real range. On its day it produces anything from slopey shoulders to fast tubes, breaking both left and right, and it earns a decent rating when the sand lines up. Skill (surfnerd): Beginner. Access (surfnerd): Getting here is the catch. You either make the long, hard paddle across the current-swept harbour entrance from Raglan, or take a boat. A boat makes the whole trip far easier and is well worth it if you can arrange one.

facts.swellExposure: NE to ESE, N to NE (surfnerd)
facts.windOffshore: SSW (surfnerd wind exposure SSE - WSW, "Offshore from SSW"); W (surfnerd guide text: "west (W) offshore wind"); South-southwest (surf-forecast)

facts.notes: Surfnerd overview: Newdicks is a punchy beach break sitting on the east side of the point from Maketu, breaking over a mix of sand and rock. Several peaks spread along the beach give you both rights and lefts to pick from, and the wave has real power, with steep drop-ins and hollow sections when it lines up. Surf-forecast Newdicks-Beach: "Newdicks Beach in Bay of Plenty is an exposed beach and reef break that only works once in a while with no particular seasonal pattern. Works best in offshore winds from the south southwest with some shelter here from west winds. Most of the surf here comes from groundswells and the ideal swell direction is from the east northeast. The beach break provides left and right handers. Best around low tide when the tide is rising. Sometimes crowded. Watch out for rocks." Access (surfnerd): Beach access here is private, so pay your way in at the honesty box before you paddle out. Other guide pins from this position: surf-forecast Newdicks-Beach 1.6 km.

facts.name: Ngarunui Beach
facts.windOffshore: SE (surfnerd wind exposure E - S, "Offshore from SE"); E (surfnerd guide text: "east (E) offshore wind"); East-southeast (surf-forecast)
facts.tide: Mid, High (surfnerd); Good surf at all stages of the tide. (surf-forecast)
hazards: A rip in the southern corner gives an armchair paddle out the back, where rolling walls stretch both ways. (surfnerd)
facts.notes: Surfnerd overview: Ngarunui Beach, also known as Wainui Beach, is tucked into the corner of Raglan Bay and almost always has something to ride for all abilities. It's the easiest place to check and surf in Raglan, with peaks breaking over sand that peel both left and right. A rip in the southern corner gives an armchair paddle out the back, where rolling walls stretch both ways. There are more peaks down towards the harbour, though a southwest wind tends to mess them up. Check: surfnerd states facing NW but best swell SW (90 degrees apart); both are as published. Skill (surfnerd): Beginner. Surf-forecast Ngarunui-Beach: "Raglan - Ngarunui Beach in Raglan and West Waikato is an exposed beach break that has very reliable surf and works all around the year. The best wind direction is from the east southeast. Groundswells are more common than windswells and the best swell direction is from the west southwest. The beach breaks offer lefts and rights. Good surf at all stages of the tide. Sometimes crowded. Take special care here if it gets very crowded." Access (surfnerd): Head in on Main Road as it becomes Bow Street, and at the first roundabout turn left onto Bankart Street. Turn left again at the next roundabout onto Wainui Road, carry on a little further, then turn right onto Wainui Reserve Road. Park at the end at Wainui Reserve and walk out onto the beach. There's a car park with free parking, along with restrooms, showers, a lifeguard, and a surf school on hand. Other guide pins from this position: surf-forecast Ngarunui-Beach 0.3 km.

facts.name: Ngunguru Bar
facts.windOffshore: NNE (surfnerd wind exposure NNW - ENE, "Offshore from NNE"); N (surfnerd guide text: "north (N) offshore wind"); Northwest (surf-forecast)
facts.tide: Low, Mid (surfnerd); Good surf at all stages of the tide. (surf-forecast)
facts.notes: Surfnerd overview: Ngunguru Bar is a left-hand river mouth break that forms over migrating sandbars where the river meets the sea. The banks shift, so the peaks along the sand spit change from session to session, but when the sand lines up it shapes a rideable left. Check: surfnerd states facing SSW but best swell E (112.5 degrees apart); both are as published. Skill (surfnerd): Intermediate. Surf-forecast Ngunguru-Bar: "Ngunguru Bar in Northland is an exposed beach break that does not work very often Offshore winds blow from the northwest. Most of the surf here comes from groundswells and the best swell direction is from the east northeast. The beach breaks consists of lefts. Good surf at all stages of the tide. Rarely crowded here. Watch out for dangerous rips." Access (surfnerd): From Whangarei, head north on Bank Street onto Mill Road, continue onto Waiatawa Road and Keripaka Road, then turn right at the big roundabout to stay on Keripaka Road. It becomes Ngunguru Road as you leave town; follow it all the way to Ngunguru and find a park near the river, where there is a car park with free parking as well as roadside parking. From there, paddle across the river mouth and walk onto the beach to reach the bar and the peaks that run down the sand spit. Other guide pins from this position: surf-forecast Ngunguru-Bar 0.5 km.

facts.notes: Surfnerd overview: Oakura is a mellow beach break that peels both left and right over a mix of uneven reef and sand. It's a good place to head for shelter from strong south winds, and it comes alive in smaller swells than some of the surrounding New Plymouth beaches and reefs. In Oakura proper you'll find a high-tide beachbreak that suits all abilities, while the multiple stream mouths can shape decent low-tide bars. When the swell gets bigger, there's a bombie out the back that can be ridden at size. Check: surfnerd states facing NW but best swell SW (90 degrees apart); both are as published. Skill (surfnerd): Beginner. Surf-forecast Oakura-Beach: "Oakura Beach in Taranaki is an exposed beach and reef break that usually has waves. Autumn and winter are the optimum times of year for waves. Offshore winds are from the southeast with some shelter here from southwest winds. Waves just as likely from local windswells as from distant groundswells and the optimum swell angle is from the west. The beach break offers both left and right hand waves. Best around high tide when the tide is rising. A fairly popluar wave that can sometimes get crowded" Access (surfnerd): From New Plymouth, head southwest on Devon Street West and carry on out of town along South Road (State Highway 45). Once you reach Oakura, turn right onto either Dixon Street or Wairau Road and follow it down to the beach. It's a patrolled beach with full facilities, including restrooms, showers, camping, a lifeguard, and a surf school, plus a surf shop for any supplies. Parking is easy, with a car park offering free parking as well as roadside spots. Other guide pins from this position: surf-forecast Oakura-Beach 1.0 km.

facts.notes: Surfnerd overview: Oamaru Harbour is a right-hand reef break that peels off the northeastern tip of the harbour, at the end of the MacAndrew breakwater. It breaks over a mix of uneven reef and sand, and it can be inconsistent, so it takes the right swell to switch on. The wave is fairly modest overall, but a fun option when the setup lines up. Skill (surfnerd): Intermediate. Access (surfnerd): From State Highway 1 heading south, veer left into the old part of town on Thames Street, then turn left onto Itchen Street, right onto Tyne Street, and left onto Arun Street. From there you can park at the end of Waterfront Road or turn onto Marine Parade to find a spot, with free roadside parking on offer. Suit up, walk out along one of the breakwaters, and paddle across to the break at the end of the point. Keep an eye out for boat traffic around the harbour entrance.

facts.notes: Surfnerd overview: Peaks is a long left-hand point break, and one of the longest single-section points in New Zealand. It breaks over a mix of uneven reef and sand, and the paddle-out between the rocky outcrops is tricky. When it's on, it holds full-speed walls, hollow pockets, and technical sections that experienced surfers can link for the full kilometre back to the beach. The take-off is a sucky launch straight into the barrel, so less-experienced surfers are better off riding the sweep down to one of the many other entry points. Check: surfnerd states facing N but best swell SW (135 degrees apart); both are as published. Skill (surfnerd): Expert. Access (surfnerd): There's a car park with free parking.

facts.name: Pegasus Bay
facts.windOffshore: W (surfnerd wind exposure SW - NW, "Offshore from W"); W (surfnerd guide text: "west (W) offshore wind")
facts.notes: Surfnerd overview: Pegasus Bay is a 50km sandy sweep offering a long string of beachbreaks and a single point. It starts in the north with a left-hand point called Fossils, reached by 4WD, then runs south through the beachbreaks at Amberley, Leithfield, Waikuku and Pines. At the southern end, the shifting bars of the Waimakariri Rivermouth pull surfers in for their lefts and rights, while whitebait fishermen work the same water. The river pushes cold, muddy water across those rivermouth peaks. Skill (surfnerd): Beginner. Access (surfnerd): The rivermouth peaks are best reached from Kaiapoi, the town on the north side. Nearby you'll find restrooms, showers and camping, plus a car park with free parking and roadside parking.

facts.name: Piha
facts.windOffshore: E (surfnerd wind exposure NE - SE, "Offshore from E"); E (surfnerd guide text: "east (E) offshore wind"); Southeast, East (surf-forecast)
facts.tide: Low, Mid, High (surfnerd); Best around low tide when the tide is rising. (surf-forecast); Best around high tide when the tide is rising. (surf-forecast)
hazards: Keep an eye on the currents: the rip is fast and furious, there's a keyhole around the rocks, and more currents flank Lion Rock, which actually helps the paddle out when it gets punishing at size. (surfnerd)
At North Piha the streams and stronger currents are dangerous and have claimed many swimmers' lives. (surfnerd)
facts.season: Autumn, most often March (surf-forecast); Autumn, most often February (surf-forecast)
facts.notes: Surfnerd overview: Piha is New Zealand's most famous surf beach, a black iron-sand stretch about 40 km / 25 mi west of Auckland. Rugged cliffs and the majestic Lion Rock frame the sand, and the scenery is dramatic from the viewpoint on the drive down. The beach is backed by the Waitakere Ranges, a protected parkland of sub-tropical forest laced with bush tracks. It has a reputation for awesome surf and holds size better than most beaches. Skill (surfnerd): Beginner. Surf-forecast Piha-The-Bar: "Piha-The Bar in West Coast Auckland is an exposed beach break that has quite reliable surf Offshore winds are from the southeast. Tends to receive a mix of groundswells and windswells and the optimum swell angle is from the southwest. The beach breaks offer left-handers. Best around low tide when the tide is rising. Sometimes crowded. Hazards include rips and rocks." Surf-forecast Piha-The-Ditch: "Piha-The Ditch in West Coast Auckland is an exposed beach break that has pretty consitent surf and can work at any time of the year. The best wind direction is from the southeast. Waves can be ok even in light onshore winds Most of the surf here comes from groundswells and the optimum swell angle is from the southwest. The beach breaks are all rights. Best around high tide when the tide is rising. It's sometimes crowded here. Hazards include rips and rocks." Surf-forecast North-Piha: "North Piha in West Coast Auckland is an exposed beach break that has fairly consistent surf and can work at any time of the year. Offshore winds blow from the east. Waves can be ok even in light onshore winds Groundswells and windswells are equally likely and the ideal swell direction is from the southwest. Prevailing left breaking waves at the beach break. Best around high tide when the tide is rising. A fairly popluar wave that can sometimes get crowded Watch out for rips and rocks." Access (surfnerd): From Auckland, head west through Glen Eden on West Coast Road, turn left onto Piha Road at Waitatarua (signposted to West Coast Beaches), and follow it to Piha; turn onto Seaview Road down to the beach and choose South Piha or North Piha. There's a South Piha Lifesaving Club and a North Piha Lifesaving Club. Facilities include restrooms, lifeguards, and a surf school, plus a car park with free parking. Note the iron-sand gets mighty hot in the sun. Other guide pins from this position: surf-forecast Piha-The-Bar 0.7 km, surf-forecast Piha-The-Ditch 1.1 km, surf-forecast North-Piha 1.5 km.

It's a good pick for intermediates after a bit of space. Check: surfnerd states facing NNE but best swell SW (157.5 degrees apart); both are as published. Skill (surfnerd): Intermediate. Surf-forecast Shipwreck-Bay-Pines: "Shipwreck Bay-Pines in Northland is a sheltered beach and reef break that has fairly consistent surf Offshore winds are from the south. Tends to receive distant groundswells and the ideal swell direction is from the southwest. Both left and right reef breaks. Best around high tide. Even when there are waves, it's not likley to be crowded. Dangerous rips are a hazard of surfing here." Access (surfnerd): There's a car park with free parking at the end of the road. From Kaitaia, head southwest out of town on Redan Street, then continue straight onto Pukepoto Road. At Ahipara, carry straight on along Foreshore Road and over the Wairoa River, where the road turns to gravel. Follow the shoreline west to the far end of the bay, turn right onto Wreck Bay Road, and drive to the end to park. Other guide pins from this position: surf-forecast Shipwreck-Bay-Pines 1.8 km.

There's a car park with free parking as well as roadside parking. Keep the strong harbour-mouth rips in mind once you're out.

facts.notes: Surfnerd overview: Shipwreck Bay is a left-hand point that peels over sand at the end of a daisy chain of lefthand points, and it ranks among New Zealand's most iconic waves. It is the mellower ride of the bunch, breaking over sandbars, but it still holds pristine, top-quality peelers that pull in everyone from rippers to improvers. Check: surfnerd states facing NE but best swell SW (180 degrees apart); both are as published. Skill (surfnerd): Beginner. Surf-forecast Shipwreck-Bay-Supertubes: "Shipwreck Bay-Supertubes in Northland is a sheltered reef break that has fairly consistent surf Offshore winds blow from the south. Tends to receive distant groundswells and the ideal swell angle is from the southwest. The beach breaks offer left-handers. Best around low tide when the tide is rising. Even when there are waves, it's not likley to be crowded. Take care of the strong rips here." Access (surfnerd): Shipwreck Bay is the closest wave to the car park and camping, making it the most accessible break in the area. You will find a car park with free parking, restrooms, and camping right by the beach. Other guide pins from this position: surf-forecast Shipwreck-Bay-Supertubes 1.4 km.

facts.name: Sky Williams
facts.windOffshore: NE (surfnerd wind exposure N - E, "Offshore from NE"); NE (surfnerd guide text: "northeast (NE) offshore wind"); East-northeast (surf-forecast)
facts.tide: Low (Best at Low, Better on rising) (surfnerd); Best around high tide. (surf-forecast)
facts.notes: Surfnerd overview: Sky Williams is a left-hand point that hugs a fringing reef and runs down a long line before tucking into a protected cove, throwing the odd barrel along the way. It breaks over uneven reef, and it shares its point with Mangahume, the right-hander on the same setup, so it is worth knowing which side you are looking at. Skill (surfnerd): Intermediate. Surf-forecast Sky-Williams: "Sky Williams in Taranaki is an exposed beach and reef break that has fairly consistent surf. Spring and Summer provide the best conditions. Offshore winds are from the east northeast. Waves just as likely from local windswells as from distant groundswells and the best swell direction is from the southwest. A choice of left and right reefs. Best around high tide. It very rarely gets crowded here. Watch out for rocks." Access (surfnerd): From New Plymouth, head south on the surf highway, State Highway 45. Continue a little south of Opunake, just past Mataikahawai Road and just before Watino Road, and park near the small stream. From there it is a walk, following the creek down to the beach where the left-hand point breaks. There is free roadside parking near the stream. Other guide pins from this position: surf-forecast Sky-Williams 6.7 km.

facts.notes: Surfnerd overview: Takapuna Reef, known locally as Taka Reef, is a reef break that peaks up in front of the boat ramp and shoulders off to the right. The beachbreaks to the south are a better call for beginners, stand-up paddlers and cruisy longboarders, though they hold little shape.

On its day the waves can stand up to almost double overhead, and there are some thrusting rights that break off the southern end. It breaks over sand and offers both lefts and rights, which makes for a fun, varied setup. Skill (surfnerd): Beginner. Surf-forecast Taupo-Bay: "Taupo Bay in Northland is a sheltered beach break that is usually a safe bet Offshore winds are from the west. Tends to receive distant groundswells and the ideal swell angle is from the northeast. Waves at the beach break both left and right. Best around mid tide. Unlikely to be too crowded, even when the surf is up. Beware of rips and rocks." Access (surfnerd): The bay sits east of Kaitaia on the Northland coast. From Whangarei, head north on Western Hills Drive (State Highway 1). At Kawakawa turn left onto Queen Street (State Highway 1), then turn right onto State Highway 10. Turn right onto Taupo Bay Road and follow it all the way down to the beach, then take Marlin Drive along the beachfront. There is a car park at the beach, and facilities include restrooms, showers, camping, and the surf school. Other guide pins from this position: surf-forecast Taupo-Bay 0.1 km.

facts.notes: Surfnerd overview: Taylors Mistake is a sand-bottomed beach break that holds more size than the beaches around it. It tends to close out when the swell is small, so it really comes into its own once there's some size running, throwing up chunky lefts and rights near the beach headlands at lower tides. It rates as a good spot overall. Skill (surfnerd): Beginner. Surf-forecast Taylors-Mistake: "Taylors Mistake in Kaikoura is a fairly exposed beach break that has reasonably consistent surf and can work at any time of the year. Works best in offshore winds from the west. Groundswells more frequent than windswells and the ideal swell direction is from the east northeast. The beach breaks offer lefts and rights. Good surf at all stages of the tide. When the surf is up, it can get quite busy in the water. Take care of rips and rocks." Access (surfnerd): From Christchurch City, head east on Moorhouse Ave onto Ferry Road and continue all the way to Sumner, then turn left onto Nayland Street. At the bottom of the hill the road bends left and becomes Heberden Ave, then Scarborough Road as it winds up and over the hill, before turning into Taylors Mistake Road on the way down the other side into the bay. There's a car park with free parking, plus restrooms, showers, a lifeguard, and a surf shop. When it's bigger, use the rips by the rocks to help you get out. Other guide pins from this position: surf-forecast Taylors-Mistake 0.5 km.

facts.notes: Surfnerd overview: Te Akau is a powerful beachbreak set on a lonely, isolated stretch of coast north of Raglan. It's a good-quality wave that breaks over sand, with scattered rocks around the peaks and noticeable currents to keep an eye on in the water. Reaching it takes a bit of effort down a gravel road, which helps keep the setting wild and remote. Skill (surfnerd): Intermediate. Access (surfnerd): A gravel road leads down to the beach, and there's free parking when you arrive. To get there, take State Highway 22 west through Glen Massey, turn left onto Te Akau Road, continue onto Te Akau Coast Road, then take the next left onto the gravel road that winds out to the beach.

The break sits just south of Mahia, a little south of The Spit.

facts.notes: Surfnerd overview: The Box is a right-hand reef break in Northland that peels over uneven reef into short, fairly cavernous tubes. Skill (surfnerd): Expert. Surf-forecast The_Box: "The Box in Northland is an exposed reef break that has very consistent surf Works best in offshore winds from the east. Groundswells more frequent than windswells and the ideal swell direction is from the southwest. No reef break here. It very rarely gets crowded here. Hazards include rocks/rips." Access (surfnerd): Access is from Wreck Bay Road. Drive to the end and find a park, then either take the long walk west around the point past Shipwreck Bay, Supertubes and Pines until you reach a blue house on the hill, or drive along the beach if you have a 4WD. The beach route is tidal and can be dangerous, so take care. Other guide pins from this position: surf-forecast The_Box 1.0 km.

facts.notes: Surfnerd overview: Three Points, also known as Marau Point, is a set of right-hand pointbreaks northeast of Gisborne that gets plenty of talk but sees little traffic. The waves peel over a mix of boulders and sand, and the quality is excellent when everything lines up. Just offshore, Motuori Island picks up rights on its north side in east swells, so there's more than one option in the area. Check: surfnerd states facing NNE but best swell SE (112.5 degrees apart); both are as published. Skill (surfnerd): Expert. Surf-forecast Three-Points: "Three Points in East Cape is an exposed beach and point break that does not work very often with no particular seasonal pattern. Offshore winds are from the southwest. Groundswells are more common than windswells and the ideal swell direction is from the east. The beach breaks offer lefts and rights Best around mid tide when the tide is falling. Relatively few surfers here, even on good days. Beware of rips and rocks." Access (surfnerd): Getting here is the main barrier. From Gisborne town centre, head east on Gladstone Road onto Wainui Road and State Highway 35 toward Wainui, then continue past Wainui on Moana Road and onto Whangara Road. Just past Tolaga Bay, turn right onto Kaiaua Road, which turns to gravel and runs down to the beach at Kaiaua. From there it's roughly a 2 km walk northeast over the point to the next bay, and you'll need the farmer's permission to cross his land. Parking is restricted. Other guide pins from this position: surf-forecast Three-Points 0.6 km.

facts.name: Tuamoto Island
facts.windOffshore: NNW (surfnerd wind exposure WNW - NNE, "Offshore from NNW"); N (surfnerd guide text: "north (N) offshore wind"); North-northeast (surf-forecast)
facts.tide: Low, Mid (surfnerd); Best around low tide when the tide is rising. (surf-forecast)
facts.notes: Surfnerd overview: Tuamoto Island is an excellent reef break that holds both lefts and rights over an uneven reef, reached only by a long paddle or a short boat ride. Long, hollow lefts peel along the southern reef at a section known as The Bowl, while shorter, more intense rights fire at Inside Island. It's a wave for expert surfers who are comfortable a long way from shore. Skill (surfnerd): Expert. Surf-forecast Tuamotu-Island: "Tuamotu Island in Gisborne is an exposed reef break that has quite reliable surf and can work at any time of the year. Offshore winds are from the north northeast. Most of the surf here comes from groundswells and the best swell direction is from the south southeast. A left hand reef break. Best around low tide when the tide is rising. Rarely crowded here. Hazards include rocks/urchins." Access (surfnerd): Getting out here takes effort: a long 1.2 km paddle from Sponge Bay, or a short boat ride if you can arrange one. To reach the launch, drive east from Gisborne town centre on Gladstone Road, onto Wainui Road and State Highway 35 towards Wainui, then head up the hill and turn right onto Sponge Bay Road, following it to the end at Sponge Bay beach. There's a car park with free parking plus roadside parking. Other guide pins from this position: surf-forecast Tuamotu-Island 0.9 km.

facts.name: Waiapu
facts.windOffshore: WNW (surfnerd wind exposure WSW - NNW, "Offshore from WNW"); NW (surfnerd guide text: "northwest (NW) offshore wind"); Northwest (surf-forecast)
facts.notes: Surfnerd overview: Waiapu is a beach break at the mouth of the Waiapu River, where punchy peaks shift around over ever-changing sand and shingle bars. The banks throw up both lefts and rights, and it holds up as a decent option when the sand lines up. Skill (surfnerd): Intermediate. Surf-forecast Waiapu-River: "Waiapu River in East Cape is an exposed river break that usually has waves and can work at any time of the year. Offshore winds blow from the northwest and there is no shelter here from cross shore breezes. Still reasonable in light onshore winds Clean groundswells prevail and the ideal swell angle is from the northeast. The river breaks peel to the left. Crowds are never a problem here. Be wary of rips - they make surfing here dangerous." Access (surfnerd): Getting here means a long drive north from Gisborne: head east out of town on Gladstone Road onto Wainui Road and State Highway 35 towards Wainui, then continue on Moana Road and Whangara Road, pushing north past Tokomaru Bay and Waipiro Bay. Turn left onto Te Araroa Road (State Highway 35), and at Tikitiki turn left to stay on Te Araroa Road before turning right onto Rangitukia Road. Finally turn right onto Beach Road, which drops you at the beach on the north side of the Waiapu River mouth. There is a car park with free parking plus roadside parking, and a 4WD helps with access on this quiet stretch. Other guide pins from this position: surf-forecast Waiapu-River 0.7 km.

facts.notes: Surfnerd overview: Wainui is a sand-bottomed beachbreak near Gisborne with a big reputation, widely regarded as one of New Zealand's most consistent waves. Not to be confused with Raglan's Wainui Beach, it's a long beach split into five distinct sections, so there's usually a peak working somewhere along it. Skill (surfnerd): Intermediate. Surf-forecast Stockroute-Wainui-Beach: "Stockroute(Wainui Beach) in Gisborne is a fairly exposed beach and reef break that is usually a safe bet and works all around the year. Offshore winds blow from the west. Groundswells are more common than windswells and the best swell direction is from the south southeast. Waves at the beach are both lefts and rights. Best around mid tide when the tide is rising. When it's working here, it can get crowded. Watch out for rips and rocks." Surf-forecast Wainui-Beach-Schools: "Wainui Beach - Schools in Gisborne and Mahia is an exposed beach and reef break that has very reliable surf and works all around the year. Offshore winds are from the northwest. Groundswells more frequent than windswells and the best swell direction is from the south southeast. Waves at the beach break both left and right. Best around mid tide when the tide is rising. When it's working here, it can get crowded. Watch out for rips and rocks." Surf-forecast Pines-Wainui-Beach: "Pines(Wainui Beach) in Gisborne is a fairly exposed beach and reef break that usually has waves and can work at any time of the year. Offshore winds are from the west. Most of the surf here comes from groundswells and the optimum swell angle is from the south southeast. Waves at the beach break both left and right. Best around mid tide when the tide is rising. When it's working here, it can get crowded. Beware of rips and rocks." Surf-forecast Wainui-Bay-Chalet: "Wainui Bay Chalet in Gisborne and Mahia is an exposed beach break that has very reliable surf and works all around the year. Ideal winds are from the northwest and there is no shelter here from cross shore breezes. Easily blown out by an onshore breeze Groundswells more frequent than windswells and the best swell direction is from the south southeast. The beach breaks offer lefts and rights. Best around low tide when the tide is rising. It's sometimes crowded here." Surf-forecast Wainui-Beach-Whales: "Wainui Beach - Whales in Gisborne and Mahia is an exposed beach and reef break that is often working and works all around the year. Works best in offshore winds from the north northwest. Clean groundswells prevail and the ideal swell angle is from the south southeast. The beach break offers both left and right hand waves. Best around mid tide when the tide is rising. It's sometimes crowded here. Watch out for rips and rocks." Access (surfnerd): From Gisborne town centre, head east on Wainui Road (Highway 35), through Kaiti and past the Sponge Bay turnoff, to reach Wainui. Park down one of the side streets with beach access or at the surf club, depending on which peak you're after. There's a car park with free parking plus roadside parking, along with restrooms and showers. facts.notes: Surfnerd overview: Waipiro Bay is a huge bay on New Zealand's east coast, with a cluster of right-hand pointbreaks at its southern end and above-average beachbreaks spread along the sand. The points break over boulders and sand, and there are rocky outcrops at the north end that hold more waves. Kitties is the inside section closer to the beach, Frog Rock is shorter and faster and ends abruptly on the rocks, and further out sits Creek, a fast, hollow wave best left to experienced surfers. It is a good, varied spot with plenty of options once it turns on. Check: surfnerd states facing NE but best swell SE (90 degrees apart); both are as published. Skill (surfnerd): Intermediate. Access (surfnerd): From Gisborne, head east on Wainui Road (State Highway 35) and continue north to Te Puia Springs, then turn right onto Waipiro Road and follow it down to Waipiro Bay. Turn right onto Waikawa Road to reach the south end of the beach, though you can find a spot anywhere along the bay. Take care on the steep gravel road in. There is camping nearby, plus a car park with free parking and roadside parking.

facts.notes: Surfnerd overview: Waitara Bar is a river-mouth break that peels over boulders and sand where the Waitara River meets the sea. It throws up both lefts and rights and holds a decent wave when it lines up. On the East Beach side, tidy A-frame peaks form, while across the river a good left can appear, and there are reefs scattered around the area too. Skill (surfnerd): Intermediate. Surf-forecast Waitara-Bar: "Waitara Bar in Taranaki is a fairly exposed beach/River Bar break that has unreliable waves. Autumn and winter are the best times of year for waves. Offshore winds are from the south southeast. Poor surf in light onshore winds Windswells and groundswells in equal measure and the best swell direction is from the west southwest. The beach breaks offer lefts and rights. Best around high tide. Unlikely to be too crowded, even when the surf is up." Access (surfnerd): From New Plymouth city centre, head east on Devon Street East and continue onto State Highway 3 out of town. Near Waitara, turn left onto Devon Street and then Nelson Street heading into town. The road bends right onto McLean Street and crosses the Waitara River. Turn left onto Leslie Street, then left onto Howard Street, which brings you to the beach on the eastern side of the river, along with the board riders club. There's a car park at the beach, and camping is available. Other guide pins from this position: surf-forecast Waitara-Bar 0.7 km.

There's a car park, plus restrooms and camping.

facts.notes: Surfnerd overview: Weld Road is an easygoing beach break near New Plymouth that sits right next to Ahu Ahu and shares much of its character. Easy, rolling peaks make it a natural pick for longboarding, learners, and lazy days, with both lefts and rights peeling over a mix of boulders and sand. It is a consistent break that reliably picks up swell, and the quality is decent when it lines up. Check: surfnerd states facing N but best swell SW (135 degrees apart); both are as published. Skill (surfnerd): Beginner. Surf-forecast Weld-Road: "Weld Road in Taranaki is an exposed reef break that has pretty consitent surf and can work at any time of the year. Works best in offshore winds from the southeast. Most of the surf here comes from groundswells and the ideal swell direction is from the southwest. A right hand reef. When the surf is up, it can get quite busy in the water. Submerged rocks are a hazard." Surf-forecast Ahu-Ahu-Road: "Ahu Ahu Road in Taranaki is an exposed beach and reef break that has quite consistent surf and can work at any time of the year. The best wind direction is from the southeast with some shelter here from southwest winds. Windswells and groundswells in equal measure and the ideal swell direction is from the west southwest. The beach breaks offer lefts and rights and there are also left and right hand reef breaks on offer.. A fairly popluar wave that can sometimes get crowded" Access (surfnerd): From New Plymouth, head southwest on Devon Street West onto South Road, the Surf Highway (State Highway 45), continue through Oakura, then turn right onto Weld Road and follow it to the end. Small tracks lead through farmland to the water, so always ask permission before crossing private property and close every farm gate behind you. You will find restrooms and camping, with free roadside parking. Other guide pins from this position: surf-forecast Weld-Road 1.3 km, surf-forecast Ahu-Ahu-Road 2.1 km.

facts.notes: Surfnerd overview: Whangapoua is a right-hand river mouth on Great Barrier Island, peeling over sand in a pristine, undeveloped setting. Surf-forecast Whangapoua-Estuary-Okiwi: "Whangapoua Estuary(Okiwi) in Great Barrier Island is a fairly exposed beach break that has quite reliable surf. Spring and Summer provide the best conditions. Best around low tide when the tide is falling. Rarely crowded here. Watch out for rips, sharks." Access (surfnerd): Getting here means taking the car ferry across to Great Barrier Island, where you can camp at one of the many spartan campsites. There are restrooms and showers on hand, plus a car park with free parking and roadside spots nearby. Other guide pins from this position: surf-forecast Whangapoua-Estuary-Okiwi 0.2 km.

Surf-forecast Whites-Bay: "Whites Bay in Nelson is a fairly exposed beach break that has very consistent waves, although summer tends to be mostly flat. The best wind direction is from the northwest. Most of the surf here comes from groundswells and the ideal swell angle is from the southeast. The beach breaks offer lefts and rights. Best around high tide. Rarely crowded here. Watch out for dangerous rips." Other guide pins from this position: surf-forecast Whites-Bay 1.3 km.

facts.notes: Surfnerd overview: Windies is an easy right-hand point that peels along a rocky point at the far end of Cape Palliser, just southeast of Craps near the Ngawi Golf Course. The wave runs for over 100m and serves up several sections to play with, so there's plenty to work with once you're on it. Surf-forecast Windies-Ngawi: "Windies (Ngawi) in The Wairarapa is an exposed reef and point break that has quite reliable surf, although summer tends to be mostly flat. The best wind direction is from the northeast with some shelter here from northeast winds. Groundswells and windswells are equally likely and the optimum swell angle is from the south. There is no beach break and there is right hand reef break too. An uncrowded break, even when it is working. Submerged rocks are a hazard." Other guide pins from this position: surf-forecast Windies-Ngawi 0.2 km.

facts.notes: Surfnerd overview: Woodpecker Bay sits on the West Coast between Punakaiki and Charleston, with the break tucked into the southern end of the bay by Seal Island. When the swell is big enough, it wraps around Seal Island and throws up big, wally waves on the inside, with both rights and lefts on offer. Surf-forecast Woodpecker-Bay: "Woodpecker Bay in West Coast South Island is a sheltered beach break that has fairly consistent surf and can work at any time of the year. The best wind direction is from the south southeast with some shelter here from south southwest winds. Tends to receive a mix of groundswells and windswells and the best swell direction is from the southwest. There is no beach break and there are also left and right reef breaks (left is best). An uncrowded break, even when it is working. Watch out for rocks." Other guide pins from this position: surf-forecast Woodpecker-Bay 1.5 km.
